title: Cardiovascular and Peripheral Vascular Disorders
markdown:
CHAPTER 9

## Cardiovascular and Peripheral Vascular Disorders

## CONTENT OVERVIEW

- Hypertension
- Dyslipidemia
- Heart failure
- Atrial fibrillation
- Anticoagulation
- Heart murmurs

## NOTES

## HYPERTENSION: MAKING THE DIAGNOSIS

- Guidelines: JNC-8 and ACC/AHA are recognized on the certification exam.
- JNC-8 does not stage HTN
- ACC/AHA stages HTN

| BP Category   | Systolic BP      |              | Diastolic BP   |
|---------------|------------------|--------------|----------------|
| Normal        | <120 mm Hg       | And          | <80 mm Hg      |
| Elevated      | 120 to 129 mm Hg | And          | <80 mm Hg      |
| HYPERTENSION  | HYPERTENSION     | HYPERTENSION | HYPERTENSION   |
| Stage 1       | 130 to 139 mm Hg | Or           | 80 to 89 mm Hg |
| Stage 2       | ≥140 mm Hg       | Or           | ≥90 mm Hg      |

## HTN: Management Goals

## ACC/AHA GOAL

## Goal <130/80

(All patients)

*Initiate pharmacotherapy when:

- >140 or >90 or
- >130 or >80 with:
- CVD
- CVA
- DM
- CKD
- ASCVD risk >7.5%

## JNC-8 GOAL

| Goal <140/90                                          |
|-------------------------------------------------------|
| <60 years old                                         |
| DM                                                    |
| CKD                                                   |
| Goal <150/90                                          |
| >60 years (without DM or CKD)                         |
| *Initiate pharmacotherapy when patient is above goal. |

*Follows 2025 ACC/AHA Guidelines updated 08/2025

## ASCVD Risk & HTN Management

How do I calculate the ASCVD risk?

Get an ASCVD risk calculator!

(Free on MD Calc: PREVENT, ASCVD risk calculator, Framingham Risk)

## ACC/AHA Guidelines : HTN

## Hypertension: First-Line Treatment

| Patient Characteristics   | First-Step Drug Therapy                 |
|---------------------------|-----------------------------------------|
| General population        | Thiazide CCB (Dihydropyridines) ACE ARB |
| CKD w/proteinuria         | ACE or ARB                              |
| DM w/ CKD or proteinuria  | ACE or ARB                              |

## Hypertension: First-Line Treatment Considerations

<!-- image -->

Tip: Beta-blockers are not first-line therapy! TIP: Beta-blockers are not first-line therapy!

## NOTES

## NOTES Hypertension: Management Strategies

| Option 1                                                       | Option 2                                                            | Option 3                                                           |
|----------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Single drug titrate to maximum dose and then add a second drug | Single drug Add second drug before achieving max dose of first drug | Initiate 2 drugs simultaneously (combination pill)                 |
|                                                                |                                                                     | Recommended in patients with Stage 2 HTN or if >20 mmHg / >10 mmHg |

## QUESTION #1

What is the best choice of monotherapy to manage hypertension in an adult without comorbidities?

| Lab        | Today       | Normal Range   |
|------------|-------------|----------------|
| BUN        | 12          | 8-25 mg/dL     |
| Creatinine | 0.9         | 0.5-1.5 mg/dL  |
| eGFR       | 85 mL/min   | >60 mL/min     |
| Potassium  | 4.5 mmol/L, | 3.5-5.1 mmol/L |
| Sodium     | 138 mmol/L  | 135-146 mmol/L |

1. 25 mg metoprolol daily (25-100 mg daily)
2. 40 mg lisinopril daily (10-40 mg daily)
3. 75 mg losartan daily (50-100 mg daily)
4. 12.5 mg chlorthalidone daily (12.5-25 mg daily)

<!-- image -->

## QUESTION #2

What should be checked at this visit if chlorthalidone is prescribed?

1. Potassium
2. Glucose
3. ECG
4. No labs needed

<!-- image -->

TIP: Also monitor renal function. Cautious use in patients with gout.

## QUESTION #3

The patient is prescribed 12.5 mg chlorthalidone daily and returns in 4 weeks with the following BP log. Which choices are reasonable? Select all that apply.

| Date        | BP     | Date        | BP     |
|-------------|--------|-------------|--------|
| 30 days ago | 136/88 | 12 days ago | 140/96 |
| 21 days ago | 142/90 | 2 days ago  | 136/92 |
| 14 days ago | 132/86 | Yesterday   | 134/86 |

1. Continue the plan for another 4 weeks.
2. Add 50 mg metoprolol tartrate BID.
3. Increase chlorthalidone to 25 mg daily
4. Add 5 mg amlodipine.

<!-- image -->

## QUESTION #4

What labs, if any, should be checked 2 weeks after initiating losartan?

1. Calcium, sodium
2. Potassium, BUN/Cr
3. Glucose, potassium
4. Labs not indicated

What if lisinopril is ordered instead?

<!-- image -->

TIP: Avoid/caution prescribing ARBs in combination with ACEs and other potassium-sparing medications.

## QUESTION #5

A 35-year-old female is diagnosed with essential hypertension. She is planning to become pregnant. Which is the best antihypertensive for this patient?

1. Benazepril
2. Losartan
3. Nifedipine
4. Chlorthalidone

<!-- image -->

## QUESTION #6

Which of the following may be a clue that the patient has secondary hypertension?

1. A systolic blood pressure that is significantly higher than the diastolic
2. Chronic use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications
3. Daily use of loratadine for seasonal allergies
4. Unable to reach blood pressure goal despite use of amlodipine

<!-- image -->

## NOTES

## NOTES

## SECONDARY HTN

Primary HTN (essential HTN) is idiopathic in etiology and the most common: 90% Secondary HTN suspected when:

- Dx of HTN prepuberty
- Resistant hypertension (using >3 agents without control)
- <30 years of age
- Nonobese
- No family history
- No risk factors for HTN
- Change in previously controlled BP/labile BP
- Concurrent electrolyte or metabolic disorder

TIP: Consider OSA, renovascular, and endocrine disorders as causes for secondary hypertension.

## QUESTION #7

The NP is evaluating a 52-year-old male for HTN follow-up. His SBP is 138 mmHg in the office. After reviewing his lipid panel, the NP's first step in managing this patient includes:

| Lab               |   Result (mg/dL) | Normal Range (mg/dL)   |
|-------------------|------------------|------------------------|
| Total Cholesterol |              225 | <200                   |
| LDL               |              122 | <100                   |
| HDL               |               39 | 40                     |
| Triglycerides     |              323 | <150                   |

1. prescribing moderate intensity statin.
2. repeating lipid panel next week.
3. calculating the ASCVD risk.
4. asking the patient about familial hyperlipidemia.

## Primary Prevention: Who Gets a Statin?

|   Group | Characteristics                                         | Recommendation                                                          |
|---------|---------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------|
|       1 | LDL >190 mg/dL (regardless of ASCVD risk estimate)      | High-intensity statin                                                   |
|       2 | Diabetes mellitus, age 40-75                            | Moderate-intensity statin High-intensity statin if increased ASCVD risk |
|       3 | ASCVD RISK: (Age 40-75; LDL ≥70-≤190 mg/dL; without DM) |                                                                         |
|         | ASCVD risk estimate ≥7.5-<20% with risk enhancer        | Moderate-intensity statin                                               |
|         | ASCVD risk estimate >20% Or Secondary Prevention        | High-intensity statin                                                   |

## Risk Enhancer

Family history of early ASCVD, LDL>160 mg/dL, CKD, metabolic syndrome, preeclampsia, HIV, RA

| High Intensity Statins   | Moderate Intensity Statins   |
|--------------------------|------------------------------|
| >50% reduction in LDL-C  | >30% reduction in LDL-C      |
| Atorvastatin 40-80 mg    | Atorvastatin 10-20 mg        |
| Rosuvastatin 20-40 mg    | Rosuvastatin 5-10 mg         |
|                          | Simvastatin 20-40 mg         |
|                          | Pravastatin 40-80 mg         |

<!-- image -->

## QUESTION #8

Which of the following is true of dyslipidemia management?

1. Statin drugs significantly reduce LDL levels and are well tolerated.
2. Ezetimibe should not be used in combination with statin drugs.
3. PCSK9 inhibitors do not significantly lower LDL.
4. Fibrates significantly reduce LDL levels and are well tolerated.

<!-- image -->

## QUESTION #9

Ms. Katz, a 64-year-old, has a medical history of hypertension. She now presents with new-onset heart failure. Which of the following physical examination signs is most consistent with heart failure?

1. Rhonchi on auscultation
2. Peripheral edema
3. Split S 2 heart sound
4. Bradypnea

## Heart Failure (HF)

- Signs and symptoms
- $ Resting tachycardia
- $ Abnormal ECG
- $ Tachypnea
- $ Crackles
- $ Diaphoretic
- $ S 3 and/or S 4
- $ PMI may be displaced.
- $ Peripheral edema may be present.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

Joshua Lanclos/APEA

## QUESTION #10

Ms. Katz's HTN has previously been controlled on amlodipine 5 mg. What is the best plan of action for this patient?

1. Stop the amlodipine and initiate lisinopril.
2. Increase the amlodipine to 10 mg.
3. Add chlorthalidone to the amlodipine.
4. Stop amlodipine, initiate a beta-blocker.

<!-- image -->

TIP: CCBs are used cautiously in heart failure because they decrease cardiac contractility.

## NOTES

## NOTES Primary Care Role in HF

## EARLY RECOGNITION!

- Identify & correct underlying cause
- $ Thyroid disorder, DM, MI, valve disorder, arrhythmias
- Reinforce lifestyle modifications.
- $ Sodium restriction, medication compliance
- Hold medications that contribute:
- $ CCBs
- $ NSAIDs
- $ Alpha-1 blockers
- $ DM meds
- Thiazolidinediones
- DPP4 inhibitors

## Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm

## ULTRASOUND: GOLD STANDARD

Risk factors:

- Age older than 65 years
- Smoking history
- Male sex greater risk than female sex
- Non-Hispanic White race
- Family history
- History of AAA or other aneurysm
- Atherosclerosis

<!-- image -->

USPSTF recommends screening (Grade B):

- Males aged 65-75
- Ever smoked

## QUESTION #11

The following patients have never been screened for AAA. Which patient is the best candidate for screening today?

1. Patient A: An 84-year-old male who smokes, with a history of congestive heart failure (CHF) and atrial fibrillation
2. Patient B: A 73-year-old male who smokes, with hypertension, DM, and a BMI of 30
3. Patient C: A 62-year-old male with a family history of AAA and hypertension
4. Patient D: A 75-year-old female with a history of HTN and SLE

<!-- image -->

## Common ECG Rhythms

- Know these rhythms!
- Be able to identify ST depression and ST elevation on ECG.
- Free website to practice: https://ekg.academy/learning-resources-free

<!-- image -->

## Atrial Fibrillation

- Most commonly treated arrythmia
- Symptoms-variable!
- $ Asymptomatic
- $ Palpitations/Tachycardia
- $ Fatigue/Weakness
- $ Dizziness/Lightheadedness
- $ Reduced exercise capacity
- $ Dyspnea
- $ Angina
- $ Syncope

## Initial work up:

- TSH
- Electrolytes
- Renal panel
- CBC
- ECG
- Echocardiogram

## QUESTION #12

A 66-year-old female reports of occasional palpitations over the last few months. Atrial fibrillation with HR 104 bpm is found on ECG. In addition to ordering labs, the NP should:

1. send the patient to the ED for immediate cardioversion.
2. calculate Well score and prescribe magnesium.
3. order coronary artery calcium (CAC) test.
4. calculate CHADS-Vasc2 score to determine need for anticoagulation.

<!-- image -->

TIP: Primary care ➔ Recognize, Work up, Anticoagulate, and Refer!

NOTES

## NOTES Atrial Fibrillation: Anticoagulation

- Nearly all patients with AF will require anticoagulation.
- DOACs preferred, warfarin may be used
- Risk/benefit scenario

## CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc

- Thromboembolic risk stratification method in nonvalvular a-fib
- Anticoagulate if score:
- $ ≥2 Males
- $ ≥3 Females

| CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc Scoring Tool 2              |    |
|----------------------------------------------|----|
| CHF                                          |  1 |
| HTN                                          |  1 |
| Age > 75 years                               |  2 |
| Diabetes mellitus                            |  1 |
| Stroke/TIA or VTE (prior)                    |  2 |
| Vascular disease (MI, PAD, or aortic plaque) |  1 |
| Age 65-74                                    |  1 |
| Sex category (Female)                        |  1 |
| Total Score=                                 |    |

* The "2" denotes 2 points in the respective CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc category

## Warfarin Dosing Adjustment Based on Goal INR

| Diagnosis                          | Optimal Therapeutic Range                                   | Length of Treatment                              | Length of Treatment                               |
|------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------|
| DVT                                | 2.0-3.0                                                     | Provoked: 3 months                               | Provoked: 3 months                                |
| PE                                 | 2.0-3.0                                                     | Unprovoked: at least 3 months (reevaluate risks) | Unprovoked: at least 3 months (reevaluate risks)  |
| Atrial fibrillation (nonvalvular)  | 2.0-3.0                                                     | Long-term anticoagulation                        | Long-term anticoagulation                         |
| Moderate/Severe mitral stenosis    | 2.0-3.0                                                     | Usually                                          |                                                   |
|                                    |                                                             | life!                                            | Warfarin is the only FDA- approved anticoagulant. |
| Mechanical valve: Mitral or aortic | 2.0-3.0 Aortic 2.5-3.5 Mitral (or AVR w/ high risk for VTE) | Life!                                            |                                                   |

TIP: Mitral Valve Replacement needs MORE (INR 2.5-3.5)

## Heart Murmurs

Sounds detected when there is turbulent blood flow through the great vessels or across a heart valve

<!-- image -->

Joshua Lanclos/APEA

## Heart Murmurs: Valves

Two valves cause nearly ALL the trouble in adults!

<!-- image -->

Joshua Lanclos/APEA

NOTES

## NOTES Stenotic vs. Regurgitant Valves

Stenotic valves do not OPEN properly. Regurgitant valves do not CLOSE properly.

## Assessment of Murmurs

You think you hear a murmur. Now what? Follow APEA's three easy steps: WHEN, WHERE, WHAT!

## Step 1: WHEN

Identify when in the cardiac cycle the murmur is heard.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

Systolic murmur: Sound occurs at the same time the carotid pulse is felt.

Diastolic murmur: Sound occurs

- between carotid pulses.

## Step 2: WHERE

Where on the chest is the sound loudest?

## Auscultation points of Murmurs

<!-- image -->

Joshua Lanclos/APEA

<!-- image -->

## Step 3: WHAT

WHAT are the associated findings?

## Symptoms

- Chest pain, shortness of breath (SOB), cyanosis, exercise intolerance, palpitations

MR. PEYTON MANNING

How did Peyton Manning become a 5-time MVP? With his

Pneumonic: Diastolic Murmurs

## "ARMS"

- AR ➔ Aortic Regurgitation

## Check Your Knowledge

## Signs

- BP change
- Thrill present
- Changes in murmur with respiration or position change (standing, squatting)

## QUESTION #13

A murmur concerning for mitral regurgitation is auscultated. Which of the following is most consistent with mitral regurgitation?

1. A harsh diastolic murmur heard best at the third ICS, associated with a thrill
2. A holosystolic murmur heard best at the fifth ICS apex, a-fib seen on ECG
3. A diastolic murmur heard best at the apex, radiates to carotid
4. A systolic murmur heard best at the apex, no change with Valsalva

<!-- image -->

NOTES

## NOTES Mitral Regurgitation

Use APEA's 3 Easy Steps

|   Step | Question                        | Answer                                                                 |
|--------|---------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------|
|      1 | Systolic or Diastolic           | Systolic                                                               |
|      2 | Where do I hear it the loudest? | Mitral listening point (4th/5th ICS, left chest, apex, mid-clavicular) |
|      3 | Associated Findings             | SOB, Fatigue, Atrial fibrillation, Heart failure                       |

## QUESTION #14

A 28-year-old female has palpitations when she takes pseudoephedrine. On examination, a midsystolic click is heard at the apex. What valve is involved?

1. Mitral
2. Aortic
3. Tricuspid
4. Pulmonic

## Mitral Valve Prolapse

Use APEA's Three Easy Steps

|   Step | Question                        | Answer                         |
|--------|---------------------------------|--------------------------------|
|      1 | Systolic or Diastolic           | Systolic                       |
|      2 | Where do I hear it the loudest? | Mitral Listening Point         |
|      3 | Associated Findings             | Palpitations, PVCs, Chest Pain |

## QUESTION #15

A 50-year-old teacher has symptomatic aortic stenosis. What findings are anticipated?

1. Intermittent chest pain and a diastolic murmur
2. Atrial fibrillation and a diastolic murmur
3. Intermittent chest pain and a systolic murmur
4. Atrial fibrillation and a systolic murmur

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## Aortic Stenosis

Use APEA's three easy steps.

|   Step | Question                        | Answer                         |
|--------|---------------------------------|--------------------------------|
|      1 | Systolic or diastolic           | Systolic                       |
|      2 | Where do I hear it the loudest? | Aortic Listening Point         |
|      3 | Associated findings             | Angina, Syncope, Heart failure |

## QUESTION #16

A 58-year-old has aortic regurgitation. What choice describes this murmur?

1. A diastolic murmur heard best near the apex
2. Systolic heard loudest near the second ICS, RSB
3. Diastolic murmur near the RSB, second ICS
4. Systolic murmur with wide fixed split S2, LSB, second ICS

## Aortic Regurgitation

Use APEA's three easy steps.

|   Step | Question                        | Answer                             |
|--------|---------------------------------|------------------------------------|
|      1 | Systolic or diastolic           | Diastolic                          |
|      2 | Where do I hear it the loudest? | Aortic listening point; Erbs point |
|      3 | Associated findings             | Angina, dizziness, CHF             |

## QUESTION #17

A patient has mitral stenosis. What is expected on auscultation?

1. A diastolic murmur best heard in the midclavicular 5th ICS that does not change with position
2. A systolic murmur with a midsystolic click best heard in the mitral listening area
3. A diastolic murmur best heard in the second right ICS with an associated click
4. A systolic murmur best heard in the midclavicular fifth ICS that changes with position

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

NOTES

## NOTES Mitral Stenosis

Use APEA's three easy steps.

|   Step | Question                        | Answer                     |
|--------|---------------------------------|----------------------------|
|      1 | Systolic or diastolic           | Diastolic                  |
|      2 | Where do I hear it the loudest? | Mitral listening point     |
|      3 | Associated findings             | Dyspnea, A-fib, hemoptysis |

## QUESTION #18

The following patients have an audible murmur. Which is most likely to have a physiologic murmur?

1. A 42-year-old patient with hypertension
2. A 14-year-old athlete
3. A 75-year-old patient with HF
4. A 33-year-old marathoner

Why?

## MURMURS: IN SUMMARY

The murmur is identified. Now what? Mr. Peyton Manning is the GOAT!

- G: Who GOES? ➔ Cardiology referral for all diastolic murmurs, systolic murmurs grade 4 to 6 and any murmur that keeps "bad company"
- O: Observe ➔ Monitor asymptomatic patients in primary care if stable and otherwise healthy.
- A: Assessment ➔ History, physical examination, ECG, 2D echocardiogram
- T: Time ➔ Understand most murmurs are asymptomatic until 40-60 years of age when heart failure develops.

## QUESTION #19

What findings are expected in a patient with peripheral artery disease (PAD)?

1. Dyspnea on exertion
2. Lower extremity pain with activity
3. Positive McMurray test
4. Abnormal monofilament testing

<!-- image -->

TIP: ABI <0.9 or >1.4 is highly suggestive of PAD.

A 14-year-old athlete
A 75-year-old patient with HF
A 33-year-old marathoner Why?

questions.stem: What findings are expected in a patient with peripheral artery disease (PAD)?
options: Dyspnea on exertion
Lower extremity pain with activity
Positive McMurray test
Abnormal monofilament testing TIP: ABI <0.9 or >1.4 is highly suggestive of PAD.
